http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03219v1.title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03219v1.abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03523v1.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03523v1.abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03868v1.title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03868v1.abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04196v1.title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04196v1.abstract: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555v1.title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03555v1.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03575v1.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03575v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04073v1.title: Computer-Use Agents Gain Little Benefit from a World Model When Conditioned on Tutorials
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04073v1.abstract: Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component -- tutorials, the judge, and the world model -- to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05036v1.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05036v1.abstract: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04315v1.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04315v1.abstract: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently.

http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04977v1.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04977v1.abstract: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03852v1.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03852v1.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04152v1.title: PACT: Certifying What Is Written in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04152v1.abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04003v1.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04003v1.abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05039v1.title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05039v1.abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03517v1.title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03517v1.abstract: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05512v1.title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05512v1.abstract: AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06049v1.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06049v1.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05759v1.title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05759v1.abstract: Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06409v1.title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06409v1.abstract: We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06543v1.title: Using Experience Twice: Dynamic Process Rubrics for Privileged Token-Level Credit Assignment
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06543v1.abstract: Agent trajectories often contain both successful decisions and failed attempts, yet optimization with sparse trajectory-level rewards struggles to identify which critical decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. We observe that meaningful distinctions among on-policy trajectories can be distilled into natural-language process rubrics and used as process supervision signals. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06434v1.title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06434v1.abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06545v1.abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06500v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05590v1.title: Verified but Vacuous: Three Failure Surfaces of LLM-Driven Verified Code Generation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05590v1.abstract: What should ``verified'' mean when evaluating LLM-generated code? Many existing pipelines report a single verification number. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05761v1.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06841v1.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06841v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05739v1.title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05739v1.abstract: Coding agents must deliver correct software while respecting users' expertise, preferences, and working conditions. Existing benchmarks increasingly incorporate interaction, yet personalized requirement fulfillment remains underexplored. We introduce PersonaCodeBench, which turns user characteristics into verifiable obligations in persona-driven multi-turn coding sessions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05731v1.title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05731v1.abstract: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06483v1.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06254v1.abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07689v1.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07595v1.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07932v1.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07599v1.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07461v1.abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07372v1.abstract: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07652v1.title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07652v1.abstract: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08417v1.abstract: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07640v1.abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07203v1.abstract: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07510v1.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) for code, which closely aligns with the practical needs of real-world software development, has sparked growing attention in repository-level code completion. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07286v1.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07876v1.abstract: Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly.
